title: IDOR in GET /invoices/<id>: an authenticated user reads other users' invoices
description: The GET /invoices/<id> handler takes the identifier from the last path segment and queries the invoice by its primary key only, without binding it to the authenticated user's owner_id. Any user with a valid session can read any other user's invoice (customer, amount and IBAN) by iterating sequential integer identifiers. Demonstrated in a sandbox: user bob (id 2) read invoice id 1, owned by alice (id 1), including her IBAN. The sibling route GET /invoices does filter by owner_id, which confirms the control exists in the design but is missing on this route. The server binds to 127.0.0.1 in source; real network exposure depends on deployment, but the authorization defect is independent of it.
root_cause: The query SELECT ... WHERE id = ? omits the owner_id predicate, so object-level authorization is not enforced on this route (BOLA / IDOR).
intended_behavior: An invoice read must be restricted to the authenticated owner: the query, or a subsequent authorization check, must require owner_id = current user, as GET /invoices already does.

trace.description: The route matches /invoices/<id> and takes invoice_id from the client-controlled last segment of PATH_INFO.
SELECT id, owner_id, customer, amount, iban FROM invoices WHERE id = ? runs with the id only, without binding owner_id to the authenticated user.

evidence.description: The query parameter is (invoice_id,); neither user["id"] nor owner_id appears in the WHERE clause.
The sibling route GET /invoices does apply WHERE owner_id = ? with (user["id"],), evidencing the control that is absent on /invoices/<id>.
The invoices table defines owner_id and iban; ids are sequential INTEGER PRIMARY KEY values, so enumeration is trivial.

conditions.description: The attacker needs a valid session (any authenticated user); no administrative role is required.
Invoices owned by other users exist; identifiers are sequential integers and enumerable.

execution.attacker_perspective: A low-trust authenticated user (bob, id 2) who should only see his own invoices.
instructions: In a no-network sandbox (bwrap: read-only source, empty environment, writes only to scratch, CPU/memory/time limits), seed the database with seed.py (users alice id 1 and bob id 2).
Invoke the WSGI application in-process: POST /login with user=bob&password=demo-password to obtain a token.
Call GET /invoices/1 presenting bob's token and observe the response.
execution.observed_result: 200 OK with {"id":1,"owner_id":1,"customer":"Acme Ltd","amount":1200.0,"iban":"DE00 0000 0000 0000 0000 01"}: bob read alice's invoice, including the IBAN, although he is not the owner.

remediation.strategy: Bind the read to the authenticated owner: add the owner_id predicate to the query, or reject with 404/403 when row["owner_id"] != user["id"]. Filtering in the query itself is preferable so no code path can return the row without the check. Consider not exposing owner_id and iban when they are not needed.

code_changes.fixed_code: row = db().execute("SELECT id, owner_id, customer, amount, iban FROM invoices WHERE id = ? AND owner_id = ?", (invoice_id, user["id"])).fetchone()

likelihood.reason: Trivial to exploit: a single GET with a sequential integer id and any valid session; no special conditions.

impact.reason: Cross-user read of financial data (amount and IBAN) of every invoice by id enumeration; no write or execution via this path.

confidence.reason: Complete source trace and the result reproduced in a sandbox with dummy two-tenant data.

sources.quote: Verify that the application ensures that data-specific access is restricted to consumers with explicit permissions to specific data items to mitigate insecure direct object reference (IDOR) and broken object level authorization (BOLA).

title: Possible cleartext transmission of credentials and tokens (no TLS in source)
description: The application is served with wsgiref.simple_server over plain HTTP, and there is no TLS, terminating proxy or deployment configuration in the repository. POST /login receives username and password in the body and returns a bearer token that is replayed on every request. If the service is exposed beyond loopback without a TLS terminator in front of it, credentials and tokens would travel in cleartext. The code only binds to 127.0.0.1:8080, so the real exposure and the presence of a TLS proxy are deployment facts not recorded in the repository.
claimed_root_cause: There is no transport encryption in source, and the repository cannot establish whether a TLS terminator protects the channel in production.

trace.description: make_server("127.0.0.1", 8080, app).serve_forever() serves plain HTTP; there is no TLS wrapper and no HTTPS redirect.

evidence.description: POST /login reads user and password from the request body.
The response returns the session token that is then sent in the Authorization header on every request.
The documentation describes the service as an API served on 127.0.0.1:8080, with no mention of TLS or a proxy.

blockers: The repository does not record whether the service is exposed beyond loopback, nor whether a TLS-terminating proxy (nginx, API gateway, service mesh) encrypts the channel in the real deployment.
There is no deployment configuration, manifest or IaC that fixes the transport mode.

validation_plan.local: Review the real environment's deployment configuration (systemd units, Dockerfile/compose, ingress manifests) to confirm whether a TLS terminator sits in front of the service and whether HTTPS is enforced.
validation_plan.deployment: The owner should observe, on the exposed environment, which scheme the service answers with (http/https), whether there is a forced redirect to HTTPS, and whether the cleartext port is reachable from outside the host.

sources.quote: Verify that TLS is used for all connectivity between a client and external facing, HTTP-based services, and does not fall back to insecure or unencrypted communications.

title: SQL injection in GET /search: q is interpolated into the statement with an f-string
description: The GET /search handler builds the SQL statement by concatenating the query-string parameter q through an f-string (WHERE owner_id = {user['id']} AND customer LIKE '%{q}%'). Because q is not parameterized, an authenticated user can alter the statement. Demonstrated in a sandbox as user bob (id 2): (1) the boolean payload "' OR 1=1 -- " nullified the owner_id filter and returned every owner's invoices; (2) a UNION payload "' UNION SELECT id, username || ':' || hex(pw_hash), 0 FROM users -- " dumped the users table with usernames and PBKDF2 hashes. owner_id is also interpolated but comes from the session (trusted), so the attack vector is q. sqlite3.Connection.execute runs a single statement, so full read (not chained write) of the data store was demonstrated.
root_cause: SQL built by string concatenation with user-controlled input (q) instead of a parameterized query; furthermore the owner filter sits inside the same injectable statement and can be nullified.
intended_behavior: All user input reaching the database must go through parameterized queries (? placeholders) so q cannot alter the statement structure or the owner_id predicate.

trace.description: q is taken from the client-controlled query string via parse_qs(QUERY_STRING).
q is interpolated into an f-string together with owner_id to form the SQL string.
db().execute(sql) runs the concatenated statement with no bound parameters.

evidence.description: sql = f"SELECT id, customer, amount FROM invoices WHERE owner_id = {user['id']} AND customer LIKE '%{q}%'": q enters with no escaping or parameter.
db().execute(sql).fetchall(): the statement is executed as-is, with no parameter tuple.
The users table stores salt and pw_hash, reachable via UNION from the same connection.

conditions.description: Requires a valid session (any authenticated user) because /search sits behind the current_user check.
Rows exist in invoices and users; the demonstration uses two dummy tenants.

execution.attacker_perspective: A low-trust authenticated user who should only be able to search among his own invoices.
payloads: GET /search?q=' UNION SELECT id, username || ':' || hex(pw_hash), 0 FROM users --
instructions: In a no-network sandbox (bwrap: read-only source, empty environment, writes only to scratch, CPU/memory/time limits), seed the database with seed.py.
Invoke GET /search in-process with the URL-encoded q value and observe the returned rows.
execution.observed_result: The boolean payload returned both owners' invoices (ids 1 and 2), bypassing the owner_id=2 filter; the UNION payload returned rows with 'alice:<hex pw_hash>' and 'bob:<hex pw_hash>', dumping the credential table.

remediation.strategy: Use parameterized queries: pass q as a bound parameter for the LIKE and keep owner_id as a parameter, so user input cannot alter the structure or the owner predicate. Do not build SQL with f-strings.

code_changes.fixed_code: rows = db().execute("SELECT id, customer, amount FROM invoices WHERE owner_id = ? AND customer LIKE '%' || ? || '%'", (user["id"], q)).fetchall()

likelihood.reason: Direct exploitation with one GET request and any valid session; a standard injection pattern with no special conditions.

impact.reason: Read of the whole store: all users' invoices (amount and IBAN) and the users table with password hashes. sqlite3.execute runs a single statement, so full read, not chained write, was demonstrated.

confidence.reason: Complete source-to-sink trace and two payloads reproduced in a sandbox with dummy data.

sources.quote: Verify that data selection or database queries (e.g., SQL, HQL, NoSQL, Cypher) use parameterized queries, ORMs, entity frameworks, or are otherwise protected from SQL Injection and other database injection attacks.
